explanations.2008-001: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; any state or federal law that conflicts with it is not valid.
explanations.2008-002: The U.S. Constitution sets up the government, divides its powers among three branches, and protects the basic rights of the people.
explanations.2008-003: The first three words of the Constitution are 'We the People,' expressing that the power of the government comes from the people.
explanations.2008-004: An amendment is a change to (or an addition of) the Constitution.
explanations.2008-005: The first ten amendments to the Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, which protect basic freedoms and rights.
explanations.2008-006: The First Amendment protects several rights and freedoms — for example, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom of the press, freedom to assemble, and freedom to petition the government.
explanations.2008-008: The Declaration of Independence announced that the colonies were free and independent from Great Britain.
explanations.2008-009: The Declaration of Independence states that all people have the rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
explanations.2008-010: Freedom of religion means you can practice any religion, or none at all, without government interference.
explanations.2008-011: The U.S. has a capitalist (free market) economy, where businesses and individuals — not the government — make most economic decisions.
explanations.2008-012: The rule of law means everyone — ordinary citizens and government leaders alike — must follow the law; no one is above it.
explanations.2008-013: The U.S. government has three branches — the legislative (Congress), the executive (the President), and the judicial (the courts).
explanations.2008-014: Power is divided among three branches, and each can check the others (checks and balances) so no single branch becomes too powerful.
explanations.2008-015: The President is in charge of the executive branch, which carries out and enforces the laws.
explanations.2008-016: Congress — the legislative branch — makes federal laws.
explanations.2008-017: The U.S. Congress has two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
explanations.2008-018: There are 100 U.S. senators — two for each of the 50 states.
explanations.2008-019: We elect a U.S. senator to serve a term of six years.
explanations.2008-020: This asks for the name of one of your state's current U.S. senators; it changes with elections and differs by where you live. Residents of D.C. and U.S. territories answer that they have no U.S. senators.
explanations.2008-021: The House of Representatives has 435 voting members, with each state's number based on its population.
explanations.2008-022: We elect a U.S. representative to serve a term of two years.
explanations.2008-023: This asks for the name of the person who currently represents your congressional district in the House; it changes with elections and differs by where you live. Residents of some territories may name that territory's nonvoting Delegate or Resident Commissioner instead.
explanations.2008-024: Each U.S. senator represents all the people of their entire state, not just one congressional district.
explanations.2008-025: Some states have more representatives than others because the number is based on population — states with more people get more seats in the House.
explanations.2008-026: We elect the President to serve a term of four years.
explanations.2008-027: We vote for President in November.
explanations.2008-028: This asks for the name of the current U.S. President, which changes with elections; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for who holds the office now.
explanations.2008-029: This asks for the name of the current U.S. Vice President, which changes with elections; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for who holds the office now.
explanations.2008-030: If the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President.
explanations.2008-031: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, the Speaker of the House becomes President.
explanations.2008-032: The President is the Commander in Chief of the U.S. military, giving them the highest authority to lead the armed forces.
explanations.2008-033: The President signs bills into law.
explanations.2008-034: The President vetoes (rejects) bills that Congress passes.
explanations.2008-035: The President's Cabinet — made up of the president's chief advisors and department heads — advises the president on issues related to their areas.
explanations.2008-036: Cabinet-level positions include the Vice President, the Attorney General, and secretaries of departments such as State, Treasury, and Defense.
explanations.2008-037: The judicial branch reviews and explains the laws, resolves disputes about what the law means, and decides whether a law goes against the Constitution.
explanations.2008-038: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States; its decisions on the law and the Constitution are final.
explanations.2008-039: The number of justices on the Supreme Court is set by law and can change, so check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the current number.
explanations.2008-040: This asks for the name of the current Chief Justice of the United States, which changes over time; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for who holds the office now.
explanations.2008-041: Powers reserved for the federal (national) government include printing money, declaring war, creating an army, and making treaties.
explanations.2008-042: Powers reserved for the states include providing schools and education, police protection, fire departments, driver's licenses, and approving zoning and land use.
explanations.2008-043: This asks for the name of the current governor of your state, which changes with elections and differs by where you live. Residents of D.C. answer that D.C. does not have a governor.
explanations.2008-044: This asks for the capital city of your state, which differs by where you live. D.C. is not a state and has no state capital; residents of U.S. territories name the capital of their territory.
explanations.2008-045: The two major political parties in the United States are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party.
explanations.2008-046: This asks for the political party of the current President, which changes with elections; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for who holds the office now.
explanations.2008-047: This asks for the name of the current Speaker of the House of Representatives, which changes with elections; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for who holds the office now.
explanations.2008-048: Four amendments to the Constitution address who can vote — for example, the 26th lets citizens 18 and older vote, the 24th abolished the poll tax, the 15th gave men of any race the right to vote, and the 19th gave women the right to vote.
explanations.2008-049: Responsibilities that only U.S. citizens must do include serving on a jury and voting in a federal election.
explanations.2008-050: Rights that only U.S. citizens have include voting in a federal election and running for federal office.
explanations.2008-051: Everyone living in the United States has certain rights protected by the Constitution — for example freedom of speech, religion, or the press, the right to assemble peacefully, and the right to petition the government.
explanations.2008-052: When we say the Pledge of Allegiance, we show loyalty to the United States and to the flag that represents it.
explanations.2008-053: When you become a U.S. citizen you promise to support and defend the Constitution and laws of the United States, to obey those laws, to serve the country when needed, and to give up loyalty to any other country.
explanations.2008-054: Citizens must be eighteen (18) years old or older to vote for President.
explanations.2008-055: Americans can participate in their democracy in many ways — for example by voting, joining a political party, helping with a campaign, joining a civic or community group, or contacting an elected official about an issue.
explanations.2008-056: The last day to send in federal income tax forms is April 15.
explanations.2008-057: All men must register for the Selective Service at age eighteen (18), and should do so between ages 18 and 26.
explanations.2008-058: Colonists came to America for reasons such as freedom, religious freedom, political liberty, economic opportunity, and to escape persecution.
explanations.2008-059: Native Americans (American Indians) lived in America before Europeans arrived.
explanations.2008-060: Africans were taken to America against their will and sold as slaves.
explanations.2008-061: The colonists fought the British over issues such as high taxes without representation, the quartering of British soldiers in their homes, and the lack of self-government.
explanations.2008-062: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence.
explanations.2008-063: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776.
explanations.2008-064: Three of the original 13 states are, for example, Massachusetts, New York, and Pennsylvania (others include Virginia, Georgia, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, North Carolina, and South Carolina).
explanations.2008-065: At the Constitutional Convention the Founding Fathers wrote the U.S. Constitution.
explanations.2008-067: Writers of the Federalist Papers include James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, and John Jay (they wrote under the shared name 'Publius').
explanations.2008-068: Benjamin Franklin is famous as an U.S. diplomat, the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention, the first Postmaster General, a writer of Poor Richard's Almanac, and a founder of the first free libraries.
explanations.2008-069: George Washington is called the 'Father of Our Country.'
explanations.2008-070: George Washington was the first President of the United States.
explanations.2008-071: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory (Louisiana) from France.
explanations.2008-072: Wars fought by the United States in the 1800s include the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Civil War, and the Spanish-American War.
explanations.2008-073: The U.S. war between the North and the South was the Civil War (also called the War between the States).
explanations.2008-074: Problems that led to the Civil War included slavery, economic differences, and disputes over states' rights.
explanations.2008-075: Abraham Lincoln freed the slaves with the Emancipation Proclamation, preserved (saved) the Union, and led the United States during the Civil War.
